issues.legal_issue: A party relying on a community custom to permit adoption of a married person must establish that custom, even where earlier decisions have recognized adoption customs among members of that community.
material_facts: The parties were members of the Jain community, and the claimed custom was that married men could be adopted.
The claimed custom was not pleaded, and the evidence did not establish its continuity, certainty, long usage, and reasonableness as a general custom applicable to the parties.

The earlier decisions cited concerned particular Jain customs or did not establish the broad custom claimed; one earlier decision had specifically cautioned that the evidence was insufficient to establish a custom of that breadth.
issues.conclusion: The claimed custom was not established, and earlier judicial recognition did not excuse the appellant from pleading and proving the custom applicable to the parties.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(a) and 10(iii) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, a married person may be adopted only if an applicable custom or usage permits it. A custom must be certain, reasonable, continuous, and long-used, and a party asserting it must prove it clearly and unambiguously. A judicial decision recognizing a custom may be relevant, but it is not indispensable; judicial notice is justified only where prior decisions in the same jurisdiction establish that the relevant persons regard the custom as binding in similar circumstances. The Court relied on Thakur Gokal Chand v. Pravin Kumari, AIR 1952 SC 231; The Collector of Madura v. Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathi, 12 MIA 397 (1868); Rup Chand v. Jambu Prasad, (1910) ILR 32 247; and Sheokuarbai v. Jeoraj, AIR 1921 PC 77.

predicates.adoption_custom_claimed: A party in an adoption dispute relied on a community custom to permit an adoption that the ordinary eligibility rules would not permit.
predicates.custom_evidence_insufficient: The party relying on the custom did not plead or prove evidence sufficient to establish the custom's scope and required characteristics.

issues.definition: When a party relies on a custom in an adoption dispute but does not plead or prove enough to establish it, the custom is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming to have been adopted bears the burden of proving the adoption, and conflicting oral evidence and unexplained suspicious circumstances may leave that burden unmet.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that he had been adopted as a married adult, but did not plead a custom permitting adoption of married persons or persons over fifteen.

The adoption claim rested principally on oral testimony and photographs; the testimony of the appellant and the priest conflicted about whether he was seated on the adopting father's lap, and the priest could not identify other examples of adoption of married persons.
The appellant continued to use his earlier name and filed income tax returns in that name, and he produced no document showing that he used his adoptive father's name after the alleged adoption.

The photographs did not show a ceremony being performed, their negatives were not produced, and other suspicious circumstances, including the adoptive mother's opposition, were not satisfactorily explained.
The trial court placed the burden on the plaintiff to disprove adoption, while the High Court found the adoption unproved; the Supreme Court upheld that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The appellant failed to plead and prove the factum of adoption, and the High Court's conclusion that he was not proved to be the adopted son was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A person asserting adoption bears a heavy burden because adoption changes the course of succession. Where documentary or other clinching evidence is absent, courts must scrutinize oral evidence cautiously; suspicious circumstances must be explained to the court's satisfaction, and conflicting or inadequate evidence may fail to establish adoption. The Court relied on Kishori Lal v. Mst. Chaltibai, AIR 1959 SC 504, and Rahasa Pandiani (dead) by LRs. v. Gokulananda Panda, AIR 1987 SC 962. Sections 10(iii) and 10(iv) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, also require an applicable custom for adoption of a married person or a person over fifteen.

rule.if: adoption_claim_disputed and married_adult_claimed_as_adoptee and enabling_custom_not_pleaded_or_proved and (oral_evidence_conflicted or adoption_evidence_lacked_documentary_support) and suspicious_circumstances_unexplained

predicates.adoption_claim_disputed: A person's asserted adoption was contested in a proceeding to determine whether the adoption took place.
predicates.married_adult_claimed_as_adoptee: The person claiming adoption was married and over fifteen when the alleged adoption occurred.
predicates.enabling_custom_not_pleaded_or_proved: The claimant did not plead or prove an applicable custom permitting adoption of a married person or a person over fifteen.
predicates.oral_evidence_conflicted: Witnesses gave conflicting accounts about material parts of the alleged adoption ceremony.
predicates.adoption_evidence_lacked_documentary_sup: The claimant relied on oral testimony without documentary or other clinching evidence establishing the adoption.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_unexplained: Circumstances casting doubt on the alleged adoption were not satisfactorily explained by the claimant.

issues.definition: When an adoption is disputed, the claimant was a married adult, no enabling custom was pleaded or proved, and the evidence is deficient and suspicious circumstances remain unexplained, the adoption is not proved.
